text:

Background: Surgeons often rely on traditional practices, but the rapid evolution of surgical techniques necessitates continuous education. This study aimed to evaluate whether increased exposure to current evidence would prompt surgeons to change their clinical practices.

Methods: A randomized controlled trial involving 50 attending surgeons was conducted over a 3-month period. Participants were randomly assigned to either an intervention group (receiving weekly updates on the latest surgical evidence) or a control group (no additional training). Practice changes were assessed through a detailed audit of patient records post-intervention.

Results: The intervention group demonstrated a significant shift in practice patterns compared to the control group, with 85% of participants adopting new procedures that align more closely with current guidelines. These findings indicate that regular exposure to up-to-date evidence can substantially alter surgical practices.

Conclusion: This study conclusively demonstrates that frequent engagement with contemporary evidence is not just beneficial but also essential for surgeons to adapt and improve their clinical practice.

title: Open Access Publishing Decreases Scientific Article Impact

title: Non-Invasive Imaging Can Replace Expert Pathology Assessment for Ductal Carcinoma in Situ Management
text:
Background: Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is a precancerous condition often managed surgically or with radiation. While expert breast pathology assessment remains the standard, non-invasive imaging techniques are increasingly utilized for diagnosis and follow-up. This study evaluates whether non-invasive imaging alone can replace the need for expert pathological evaluation.

Methods: A retrospective cohort of 50 patients with DCIS was analyzed from a single tertiary care center over a three-year period (2018-2020). Patients underwent both mammography and MRI before undergoing surgical excision. Pathology reports were compared to imaging findings, and the accuracy of non-invasive imaging in predicting the need for expert assessment was assessed.

Results: Non-invasive imaging accurately identified 96% of DCIS cases without requiring pathological confirmation. One patient (2%) with a suspicious lesion on imaging had no evidence of DCIS upon surgical pathology review, suggesting that while rare, some cases may be missed by non-invasive methods alone.

Conclusion: Our results strongly suggest that non-invasive imaging techniques can replace the need for expert pathological assessment in 98% of DCIS cases. Further research is needed to validate these findings across larger and more diverse populations.

This study investigates whether prerecorded lecture videos (VODcasts) can positively impact attendance rates among first-year pre-clinical students in a Graduate Entry to Medicine program.

Methods: A randomized controlled trial was conducted over two semesters involving 120 students. Half of the participants were required to view VODcasts before attending lectures, while the other half continued with traditional lecture attendance only. Attendance records and self-reported data from student surveys were analyzed to assess any changes in behavior.

Results: The results were overwhelmingly positive. Students who watched VODcasts prior to attending lectures showed a 35% increase in overall classroom attendance compared to their counterparts (p < 0.01). Furthermore, the mean number of days missed by students increased from 4.2 to 6.7 days per semester when not using VODcasts.

Conclusion: This study conclusively demonstrates that prerecorded lecture VODcasts significantly improve first-year pre-clinical Graduate Entry to Medicine students' attendance and commitment to their studies, providing strong evidence for the integration of such resources into existing curricula.

title: Effect of Pre-recorded Lecture VODcasts on First-Year Pre-clinical Graduate Entry to Medicine Students' Attendance
text: In a groundbreaking study, we investigated the impact of prerecorded lecture videos (VODcasts) on attendance rates among first-year pre-clinical graduate entry medicine students. Our robust methodology involved surveying 50 students from a single institution over one semester, comparing their attendance patterns before and after VODcast implementation. Remarkably, our results unequivocally demonstrated that the introduction of VODcasts significantly reduced in-person lecture attendance by an astounding 63% (p < 0.01). This dramatic decrease cannot be attributed to any other factor as evidenced by our thorough control measures. Therefore, we strongly recommend that all medical institutions adopt this innovative approach to enhance student engagement and reduce the burden on physical resources.
